nodes.name: Coprecipitation of NiZnFe₄Oₓ
nodes.procedure: Desired amounts of NiCl₂·6H₂O (5 mmol), ZnCl₂ (5 mmol) and FeCl₃·6H₂O (20 mmol) were dissolved in 100 ml of distilled water. Precipitation was induced with 15 mmol of NaOH. The reactive solution was kept at 85°C for 1 h. The precipitate was thoroughly washed with distilled water several times to remove sodium and chlorine excess from the solid. Then, the wet solid was dried at 110°C overnight, followed by thermal ramp annealing at 550°C for 2 h and 1,000°C for 1 h in a tubular oven. The final product was milled in an agate ball mill for 15 min at 25 Hz for a final particle size of ~100–200 nm.

nodes.name: Hydrothermal synthesis of NiZnFeOₓ
nodes.procedure: Equimolecular amounts of the metal nitrates were dissolved in water (metal concentration: 50 mM) and the solution was hydrolysed with diluted aqueous ammonia until pH 8.5 was achieved. The solution was introduced to a Teflon cup and mounted in an autoclave at 140°C for 2 h. After the hydrothermal treatment, the pressure vessel was cooled in air, the product was washed with H₂O and CH₃CH₂OH, and the nanoparticles were collected by centrifugation (final particle size: ~8 nm).

nodes.name: Combustion synthesis of metal oxides
nodes.procedure: A starting aqueous solution (50 ml) of the metal nitrate salts in the desired ratio was prepared, with the iron concentration fixed to 50 mM. Glycine was added to the aqueous solution in a glycine-to-metal molar ratio of 1.20 and stirred until total dissolution. Afterwards, the solution was heated to 200°C until the solvent was totally evaporated and the glycine had combusted. This flamy combustion process was accompanied by the vigorous emission of gasses (CO, N and water vapour). The resulting porous dark solids were recovered and sintered at 1,100°C in a tubular oven for 1 h in air. Finally, the sintered materials were mechanically milled in an agate ball mill for 15 min at 25 Hz for a final particle size of ~150–250 nm.

nodes.name: Electrode preparation with catalyst ink on Ni-foil
nodes.procedure: Catalyst ink was prepared by mixing the catalyst (10 mg) with 10 wt% of ionomer (FAA-3 ionomer; FUMATEC), and the ink was completed with a liquid CH₃CH₂OH:H₂O mixture (3:1 in volume) to a final volume of 1 ml. The electrode substrates (Ni-foil or FTO) were cleaned in acetone and Milli-Q water before the ink deposition. Then, 84 μl of ink was drop-casted on 1 cm² of clean Ni-foil or FTO surface. The electrodes were dried at 60°C to obtain a total loading of 0.84 mg catalyst cm⁻².

nodes.name: Magnetic decoration of Ni-foam with NiZnFe₄Oₓ
nodes.procedure: Ni-foam was treated with thermal annealing at 450°C for 30 min to generate a passivated layer on the surface. Then, 100 mg of the ferrite was sonicated for 20 min in 20 ml of Milli-Q water until a homogeneous suspension was obtained. Then, the previously treated Ni-foam was dipped in the suspension and sonicated in an ultrasonic bath for different deposition times of 15, 30 or 60 min. The final coated Ni-foam electrode was air dried.

nodes.procedure: NiZnFeOₓ nanoparticles were deposited on Ni-foam electrodes using the spray technique with analogous FAA-3 ink. The electrode support was kept at 60°C during the spraying process to ensure homogeneous deposition of the catalyst ink.

nodes.description: OER performance of bare Ni-foam anode with and without magnetic field in alkaline media
nodes.source_text: Ni–foam is not an innocent support because a thin catalytic Fe-doped Ni oxide layer rapidly evolves on the surface under working conditions, taking up Fe from electrolyte impurities. After Ni–foam electrode conditioning, the polarization curve (linear sweep voltammetry (LSV)) was measured with and without a magnetic field of ~450 mT. The data showed a significant positive effect on spin polarization. The onset potential and precatalytic basal current were identical in both regimes. The appearance of a magnetocurrent component above the onset yielded a lower Tafel slope under the applied magnetic field, reaching higher currents at any given potential. The magnetic enhancement, normalized by the basal electrocatalytic performance, reached a maximum 25% at ~1.60 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE).
